questions.q: What is the primary function of flowers in angiosperms (flowering plants)?
a: To produce seeds through sexual reproduction
To absorb water and mineral salts from soil
To anchor the plant firmly against strong winds
To perform all cellular respiration

questions.q: Which part of a flower consists of the anther and the filament, forming the male reproductive organ?
a: The carpel
The stamen
The sepal
The receptacle

questions.q: What is the name of the female reproductive structure of a flower consisting of the stigma, style, and ovary?
a: The stamen
The sepal
The carpel (or pistil)
The pollen tube

questions.q: Which part of the stamen produces and releases pollen grains containing male gametes?
a: The filament
The petal
The sepal
The anther

questions.q: What is the sticky surface at the top of the carpel that catches pollen grains during pollination?
a: The style
The stigma
The ovary
The ovule

questions.q: What is pollination defined as in flowering plants?
a: The fusion of male and female nuclei
The transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma
The scattering of mature seeds away from parent plants
The growth of a new root system

questions.q: Which feature is typically characteristic of insect-pollinated flowers compared to wind-pollinated flowers?
a: Large, brightly colored petals and scent with nectar
Dull green, feather-like stigmas hanging outside
No petals and massive amounts of smooth pollen
Absence of any reproductive organs

questions.q: How are pollen grains of wind-pollinated plants generally adapted for their purpose?
a: They are heavy, sticky, and spiked to cling to fur
They are produced in vast quantities, light, smooth, and easily carried by air currents
They are brightly colored and scented to attract bees
They are too large to move without mechanical pumps

questions.q: What happens immediately after a compatible pollen grain lands on the stigma of a flower?
a: It grows a pollen tube down through the style to the ovary
It turns into a green leaf
It falls off and dies instantly
It absorbs water and grows roots

questions.q: What is fertilization in flowering plants?
a: The transfer of pollen between different flowers
The fusion of the male gamete nucleus with the female gamete nucleus inside an ovule
The swelling of petals after rain
The germination of a seed in soil

questions.q: After fertilization takes place, what do the ovules and the ovary develop into respectively?
a: Leaves and stems
Seeds and fruit
Roots and root hairs
Petals and sepals

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of seed dispersal away from the parent plant?
a: To reduce competition for light, water, and mineral nutrients with the parent plant
To ensure all seeds are eaten by herbivores
To keep seeds close together for warmth
To prevent germination from ever occurring

questions.q: Which method of seed dispersal is typically used by plants like dandelions and sycamores?
a: Animal ingestion and excretion
Wind dispersal using parachute or wing structures
Explosive pod splitting
Water flotation

questions.q: How are seeds with hooks, burrs, or sticky coats usually dispersed?
a: By floating down rivers
By catching on the fur of passing animals
By wind currents in storms
By underground worms

questions.q: What environmental conditions are strictly required for a dry seed to break dormancy and begin germination?
a: Bright direct sunlight, high heat, and dry soil
Water, oxygen, and a suitable warm temperature
Carbon dioxide gas only
Freezing cold and total darkness

questions.q: Why is oxygen necessary for seed germination?
a: To power aerobic respiration, providing energy for rapid cell division and growth
To turn the seed coat green
To dissolve the seed shell with acid
To perform photosynthesis inside dark soil

questions.q: What is the role of the food store (cotyledon or endosperm) inside a seed during early germination?
a: To capture sunlight underground
To provide stored nutrients (starch, oils, proteins) until the young seedling can photosynthesize
To act as a heavy anchor against wind
To attract pollinating insects

questions.q: Which part of the plant embryo emerges first during successful seed germination?
a: The plumule (future shoot)
The radicle (future root)
The bright flower bud
The seed coat

questions.q: What is asexual reproduction in plants, and how does it differ from sexual reproduction?
a: It involves flowers and two parents fusing gametes
It produces genetically identical offspring (clones) from a single parent without gamete fusion
It requires pollination by insects
It only happens in underwater algae

questions.q: Which of the following is a natural method of asexual reproduction in plants?
a: Pollen tube growth
Runner (stolon) formation in strawberry plants
Seed dispersal by wind
Starch digestion in leaves

questions.q: What are artificial methods used by horticulturists to clone plants asexually?
a: Cuttings, grafting, and micropropagation (tissue culture)
Cross-pollination by hand
Soaking seeds in saltwater
Freezing flower buds

questions.q: What advantage does asexual reproduction offer a plant species compared to sexual reproduction?
a: It allows rapid colonization of an area with successful genetic traits when conditions are stable
It introduces wide genetic variation
It requires two different parent plants
It relies entirely on insect migration

questions.q: What is the main advantage of sexual reproduction in plants over asexual reproduction?
a: It produces genetically diverse offspring that can better adapt to environmental changes or disease
It is much faster and requires less energy
It creates identical clones every time
It does not need any water

questions.q: What is the function of bright petals in insect-pollinated flowers?
a: To protect the developing bud
To attract specific insect pollinators like bees and butterflies
To absorb mineral ions
To perform photosynthesis

questions.q: What are sepals, and what is their primary role before a flower opens?
a: Green, leaf-like structures that protect the unopened flower bud
Sticky pads that trap pollen
Tubes that transport water to petals
Sweet nectar glands

questions.q: Which part of the carpel enlarges and ripens into a fruit after fertilization is complete?
a: The stigma
The ovary wall
The filament
The sepal

questions.q: What happens to the petals and stamens of a flower after fertilization has occurred?
a: They grow larger and turn green
They wither and fall off as they are no longer needed
They turn into seeds
They burrow underground

questions.q: How do succulent fruits (like berries or apples) aid in seed dispersal by animals?
a: Animals eat the sweet fruit and pass or drop the indigestible seeds far away
Animals use them to build nests underground
Fruits explode when touched by animals
Animals carry them on their fur using hooks

questions.q: What is mechanical or explosive seed dispersal?
a: Seeds being blown by hurricanes
Seed pods drying out, splitting violently, and flinging seeds away from the parent plant
Seeds floating down rivers
Animals burying nuts in the ground

questions.q: Why do seeds enter a period of dormancy (resting stage) before germination?
a: To allow time for safe dispersal and to survive harsh or unfavorable environmental conditions
To rot away completely in soil
To turn into animal food
To consume all stored water

questions.q: What role does water play when it enters a dormant seed during imbibition?
a: It activates enzymes stored in the seed to break down food reserves and starts metabolic processes
It drowns the embryo permanently
It turns the seed into a leaf immediately
It freezes the internal cells

questions.q: What is the scientific term for the young shoot that develops from a germinating seed?
a: The radicle
The plumule
The cotyledon
The hypocotyl

questions.q: Why are wind-pollinated flowers typically lacking in scent and bright petals?
a: They do not need to attract animal pollinators, relying instead on air currents
They are dead flowers
They produce too much nectar instead
They grow entirely underground

questions.q: What is cross-pollination?
a: Transfer of pollen from an anther of one plant to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species
Transfer of pollen within the exact same flower
Fusion of two different plant species
Pollination carried out by water only

questions.q: What is self-pollination?
a: Transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant
Transfer of pollen to a completely different plant species
Pollination without any flowers
Pollen dispersal by wind across continents

questions.q: Which plant organ contains the female gametes (egg cells) inside protective structures?
a: The anther
The ovule inside the ovary
The stem node
The root tip

questions.q: What structural adaptation do many water-dispersed seeds or fruits possess?
a: Air spaces, fibrous husks, or waterproof outer coats that allow them to float
Heavy lead weights to sink immediately
Sharp metal-like thorns
Bright neon glow

questions.q: During seed germination, why does the seedling rely on stored food before its leaves break through the soil surface?
a: It cannot perform photosynthesis yet because there is no light underground
Leaves are toxic to young plants
Roots absorb all sunlight
Stored food is poisonous after germination

questions.q: What is micropropagation (tissue culture) used for in modern plant biology?
a: To produce thousands of genetically identical disease-free plant clones rapidly from small pieces of plant tissue
To crossbreed wild animals with plants
To test soil pH levels
To measure transpiration rates

questions.q: Which characteristic distinguishes angiosperms (flowering plants) from non-flowering plants like ferns and mosses?
a: They produce flowers and enclose their seeds within fruits
They reproduce exclusively using swimming sperm cells
They lack any vascular tissue
They live only in total darkness
